passages.original: evangelista, quia 280 librum Evangelii condidit, quod excepto Mattheo, alii ex duodecim apostoli non fecerunt. Propheta : vidit enim in Pathmos insula, in qua fue- rat a Domitiano principe ob Domini martyrium re- legatus, Apocalypsim infinita futurorum mysteria continentem. Refert autem Tertullianus, quod Ro- mae 2 missus in ferventis olei dolium, purior et vegetior exiverit, quam intraverit. Sed et ipsum ejus Evangelium multum distat a caeteris. Matthaeus quasi de homine incipit scribere : Liber generatio- nis Jesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham (Matth.I, 1);
passages.english: an evangelist, because he composed a book of the Gospel, which, apart from Matthew, the others of the twelve apostles did not do; a prophet, for on the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished by the emperor Domitian for his martyr's witness to the Lord, he saw the Apocalypse, which contains boundless mysteries of things to come. Tertullian, moreover, reports that at Rome he was put into a jar of boiling oil and came out purer and more vigorous than he went in. But his Gospel itself also differs greatly from the rest. Matthew begins to write as though about a man: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1);
passages.notes: The numerals 280 and 2 are page and footnote marks and have been omitted.

passages.original: Quem jamjamque capiendum uxor intelligens, exstorsit acinacem de manu, et latus ejus transverberavit. Compositoque ex more cadaveri se moriens superjecit, ne post virginalia foedera alterius coitum sustineret. Xenophon in Cyri majoris scribit infantia, occiso Abradote 1 viro, quem Panthea uxor miro amore dilexerat, collocasse se juxta corpus lacerum, et confosso pectore, san- guinem suum mariti infudisse vulneribus. Justam causam regis occidendi putavit uxor, quam mari- tus nudam 2 amico suo et ignorantem monstrave- rat.
passages.english: His wife, realizing that he was on the very point of being captured, wrenched the scimitar from his hand and ran it through his side. And when the corpse had been laid out according to custom, she threw herself, dying, upon it, so as not to endure intercourse with another after her virgin compact. Xenophon writes in the Childhood of Cyrus the Elder that, when her husband Abradates had been killed, Panthea, his wife, who had loved him with a wonderful love, laid herself beside his mangled body and, having stabbed her breast, poured her own blood into her husband's wounds. A wife thought it just cause for killing a king that her husband had shown her, naked and unaware, to his friend.
passages.notes: "Childhood of Cyrus" renders Jerome's title for the Cyropaedia. The last sentence refers to the story of Candaules' wife (Herodotus), though she is not named here.

passages.original: Marcella major ro- gata a matre sua gauderetne se nupsisse, respondit : Ita valde, ut amplius nolim. Valeria Messalarum soror, amisso Servio viro, nulli volebat nubere. Quae interrogata cur faceret, ait sibi semper maritum Servium vivere.
passages.english: Marcella the Elder, when asked by her mother whether she was glad to have married, replied: "So very glad that I want no more of it." Valeria, the sister of the Messallas, having lost her husband Servius, was unwilling to marry anyone. When she was asked why she did so, she said that for her, Servius her husband was always alive.
passages.notes: "ro- gata" is a line-break split of "rogata". "Ita valde, ut amplius nolim" is ambiguous: it may mean she was so content that she wanted no further marriage, or so 'glad' (ironically) that she wanted no more of marriage. The first sense is perhaps likelier in context, but it is uncertain.

passages.original: querulos, ira- cundos, temerarios, dure imperiosos, serviliter blandos, omnibus inutiles, ipsi novissime amori fa- cit. Nam cum fruendi cupiditate insatiabilis flagrat, plura tempora suspicionibus, lacrymis, conquestio- nibus perdit; odium sui facit, et ipse novissime sibi odio est 1. Tota amoris insectatio apud Platonem (in Phaedro) exposita est; et omnia ejus incommoda Lysias explicat, quod non judicio, sed furore du- catur : et maxime uxorum pulchritudini gravissimus custos accubet. Refert praeterea Seneca cogno- visse se quemdam ornatum hominem, qui exiturus in publicum, fascia uxoris pectus colligabat, et ne puncto quidem horae praesentia ejus carere poterat; potionemque nullam, nisi alternis [Al.
passages.english: it makes [men] querulous, irascible, rash, harshly domineering, servilely fawning, useless to everyone, and finally to love itself. For when it burns insatiably with the desire for enjoyment, it wastes more time in suspicions, tears and complaints; it makes itself hated, and in the end is hateful to itself. The whole attack on love is set out in Plato (in the Phaedrus), and Lysias explains all its drawbacks: that it is led not by judgement but by frenzy, and that above all it lies as a most oppressive guard beside the beauty of wives. Seneca further relates that he knew a certain distinguished man who, when about to go out in public, bound his wife's breast-band to himself, and could not do without her presence even for a moment of an hour; and no drink, unless by turns [another reading:
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off mid-variant note; it continues in the following context (husband and wife drank only what the other's lips had touched). "fascia uxoris pectus colligabat" is awkward; probably he tied his wife's band around his own chest.

passages.original: Segmenta eboris in medelas 3 varias assu- muntur. Fel hyaena oculorum restituit claritatem, et stercus ejus et canum putrida curat vulnera. Et (quod forsitan legendum mirum sit) hominis fimus quantis curationibus proficiat, Galenus (??)(??) ά- πλοι(??) docet. Aiunt 332 Physici, quod pellis colubri, qua exuitur, decocta in oleo, mire dolo- rem aurium mitiget. Quid ita inutile videtur ne- scientibus ut cimices? Si sanguisuga faucibus hae- serit, fumo ejus excepto, statim evomitur : et diffi- cultas urinae hujus appositione laxatur.
passages.english: Shavings of ivory are taken as various remedies. The gall of the hyena restores clearness to the eyes, and its dung and that of dogs cures putrid wounds. And (what may perhaps be surprising to read) Galen teaches in his [work on] simples how many cures human dung is useful for. Natural philosophers say that the skin of a snake, which it sheds, boiled in oil, wonderfully soothes earache. What seems so useless to the ignorant as bedbugs? If a leech has stuck in the throat, when the smoke of them is inhaled it is at once vomited out; and difficulty in urinating is relieved by applying them.
passages.notes: The Greek title of Galen's work is garbled in the scan (apparently a reference to his work on simple drugs, perhaps 'haploi...'); rendered by sense.

passages.original: gruis], ciconiae, fel aquilae, sanguis accipitris, struthiocamelus, ranae, chamaeleontes, hirundinis stercus, et carnes, quibus morbis aptae sint, dice- rem, si mihi propositum esset de medela corporum disputare. Legat qui vult Aristotelem et Theo- phrastum prosa, Marcellum Sidetem 4, et nostrum Flavium hexametris versibus disserentes : Plinium quoque Secundum, et Dioscoridem, et caeteros tam physicos quam medicos, qui nullam herbam, nullum lapidem, nullum animal tam reptile, quam, volatile, et natatile, non ad suae artis utilitatem referunt.
passages.english: cranes, storks, the gall of an eagle, the blood of a hawk, the ostrich, frogs, chameleons, swallow's dung, and flesh — for which diseases they are suitable I would tell, if it were my purpose to discuss the healing of bodies. Let whoever wishes read Aristotle and Theophrastus, who discuss [these things] in prose, and Marcellus of Side and our own Flavius in hexameter verse; also Pliny Secundus and Dioscorides and the rest, both natural philosophers and physicians, who relate no herb, no stone, no animal, whether creeping, flying or swimming, that they do not refer to the usefulness of their art.
passages.notes: Begins with a variant note fragment "gruis]" (crane, singular). "Flavius" is not certainly identifiable.

passages.original: Manduca et bibe, et si tibi placet, cum Israele lude consurgens, et canito : Manducemus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur (I Cor. XV, 32). Manducet et bibat, qui post cibos exspectat interitum; qui cum Epicuro dicit : Post mortem nihil est, et mors ipsa nihil est. Nos Paulo credimus intonanti : Esca ventri, et venter escis· Deus autem et hunc et illam destruet (I Cor. VI, 13).
passages.english: Eat and drink, and if you please, rise up with Israel to play, and sing: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die" (1 Corinthians 15:32). Let him eat and drink who after his food expects annihilation, who says with Epicurus: "After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing." We believe Paul when he thunders: "Food for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other" (1 Corinthians 6:13).

passages.original: 11. Oratione suasoria ad artes cap. ultimo. Grandis exsultatio animae unde sit. Tenuior victus, Exempla frugalitatis. Hippocrates in Aphorismis docet crassa et obesa corpora, quae crescendi mensuram comple- verint, nisi ablatione sanguinis cito imminuantur, in paralysim) et pessima morborum genera erumpere; et idcirco esse necessariam demptionem, ut rursum habeant in quae possint crescere.
passages.english: 11. [Galen] in his Exhortation to the Arts, last chapter. Whence comes great exultation of soul. A sparer diet. Examples of frugality. Hippocrates teaches in the Aphorisms that thick and fat bodies which have reached the full measure of growth, unless they are quickly reduced by drawing off blood, break out into paralysis and the worst kinds of diseases; and that therefore a reduction is necessary, so that they may again have room into which they can grow.
passages.notes: The opening lines are section headings/summary from the edition; the first is elliptical.

passages.original: — Di- caearchus in libris Antiquitatum, et descriptione Graeciae, refert sub Saturno, id est, in aureo sae- culo, cum omnia humus funderet, nullum come- disse carnes, sed universos vixisse frugibus et po- mis, quae sponte terra gignebat. Persarum rogis Cyri vita Xenophon octo voluminibus explicat : polenta et cardamo et sale ac pane cibario eos asserens victitare. Lacedaemoniorum mensae fru- galitatisque, et suprascriptus Xenophon et Theo- phrastus, et omnes pene scriptores Graeciae testes sunt.
passages.english: Dicaearchus, in his books of Antiquities and his Description of Greece, relates that under Saturn, that is, in the golden age, when the ground poured forth everything, no one ate meat, but all lived on grain and fruits which the earth produced of itself. Xenophon sets out the life of Cyrus king of the Persians in eight volumes, asserting that they lived on barley-meal, cress, salt and coarse bread. Of the table and frugality of the Spartans, both the aforementioned Xenophon and Theophrastus and nearly all the writers of Greece are witnesses.
passages.notes: "Persarum rogis" is read as "Persarum regis" (of the king of the Persians).
